en.title: WeDetect: Fast Open-Vocabulary Object Detection as Retrieval
en.abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to detect arbitrary classes via text prompts. Methods without cross-modal fusion layers (non-fusion) offer faster inference by treating recognition as a retrieval problem, \ie, matching regions to text queries in a shared embedding space. In this work, we fully explore this retrieval philosophy and demonstrate its unique advantages in efficiency and versatility through a model family named WeDetect: (1) State-of-the-art performance. WeDetect is a real-time detector with a dual-tower architecture. We show that, with well-curated data and full training, the non-fusion WeDetect surpasses other fusion models and establishes a strong open-vocabulary foundation. (2) Fast backtrack of historical data. WeDetect-Uni is a universal proposal generator based on WeDetect. We freeze the entire detector and only finetune an objectness prompt to retrieve generic object proposals across categories. Importantly, the proposal embeddings are class-specific and enable a new application, object retrieval, supporting retrieval objects in historical data. (3) Integration with LMMs for referring expression comprehension (REC). We further propose WeDetect-Ref, an LMM-based object classifier to handle complex referring expressions, which retrieves target objects from the proposal list extracted by WeDetect-Uni. It discards next-token prediction and classifies objects in a single forward pass. Together, the WeDetect family unifies detection, proposal generation, object retrieval, and REC under a coherent retrieval framework, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 15 benchmarks with high inference efficiency.

summary.summary: WeDetect introduces a retrieval-based framework for open-vocabulary object detection, universal proposal generation, and referring expression comprehension, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy while maintaining real-time inference speeds. The framework processes objects in parallel, significantly outperforming fusion-based and sequential decoding methods in efficiency.
originalProblem: Existing open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) methods using deep cross-modal fusion layers suffer from significant computational overhead and slow inference speeds.
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) for referring expression comprehension (REC) struggle with precise bounding box regression and slow inference due to sequential next-token prediction.
Prior non-fusion (dual-tower) OVD methods, while efficient, often lacked the fine-grained vision-language alignment and accuracy of fusion-based approaches.
solution: The WeDetect framework employs a dual-tower, non-fusion architecture, treating open-vocabulary recognition as a fast retrieval problem in a shared embedding space.
A massive, high-quality grounding dataset with 330 million bounding box annotations was curated using an automatic objectness detector and a fine-tuned MLLM for hierarchical label generation.

WeDetect-Ref reformulates REC as a retrieval task within an LLM, processing multiple object proposals in parallel with a binary classification head, bypassing sequential decoding and improving localization accuracy.
keyInsights: A well-designed non-fusion dual-tower architecture, combined with meticulous data curation and staged training, can achieve state-of-the-art OVD performance with real-time inference speed, challenging the necessity of deep cross-modal fusion.
Re-framing referring expression comprehension as an LLM-based retrieval problem allows for a 13x speedup compared to traditional sequential decoding while improving accuracy.

Universal object proposal generation and fine-grained object retrieval can be effectively achieved by freezing a powerful detector and training a single learnable objectness prompt, enabling new applications like local object search.
results: WeDetect-Tiny achieves 31.4 AP on LVIS at 62.5 fps, surpassing YOLO-World-L by 2.0-4.6 AP while being faster and smaller, demonstrating superior efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.
WeDetect-Large achieves 49.4 AP on LVIS, outperforming LLMDet by 7.4 AP and T-Rex2 by 3.6 AP, and is 3-6 times faster than Grounding-DINO.
WeDetect-Ref 4B achieves an average score of 93.2 on RefCOCO/+/g with a 13x speedup over Qwen3-VL 4B, and is the first LMM to exceed 50 AP on the COCO dataset (50.0 AP).

en.overview:
## Introduction

Object detection has evolved from traditional closed-set classification to more flexible open-vocabulary approaches that can detect arbitrary object classes specified through text descriptions. The research paper "WeDetect: Fast Open-Vocabulary Object Detection as Retrieval" introduces a comprehensive framework that treats visual recognition as a retrieval problem, enabling both high accuracy and real-time performance across multiple vision-language tasks.

The WeDetect family consists of three specialized models: WeDetect for open-vocabulary object detection, WeDetect-Uni for universal proposal generation and object retrieval, and WeDetect-Ref for referring expression comprehension using large language models. This unified approach demonstrates that retrieval-based methods can achieve state-of-the-art results while maintaining computational efficiency that existing fusion-based approaches struggle to match.

![WeDetect Architecture Overview](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12309v1/img-0.jpeg)
*Figure 1: The core WeDetect architecture employs a dual-tower design with separate text and vision encoders, performing object classification through contrastive learning without computationally expensive cross-modal fusion layers.*

## The Retrieval-Based Methodology

The fundamental innovation of WeDetect lies in its commitment to treating object recognition as a retrieval problem rather than relying on deep cross-modal fusion. Traditional open-vocabulary detection methods like Grounding-DINO achieve high accuracy through intensive fusion layers that blend visual and textual features, but this approach comes at a significant computational cost, often requiring multiple seconds per image for inference.

WeDetect employs a dual-tower architecture where visual and textual representations are processed separately and matched in a shared embedding space. The visual encoder utilizes a ConvNeXt backbone with a CSPRepBiFPAN neck, while the text encoder uses XLM-RoBERTa. Classification occurs through simple dot product operations between region features and text embeddings, eliminating the need for query-specific feature computation.

This architectural choice enables crucial efficiency gains. Visual features can be computed once and reused across multiple text queries, making the system particularly well-suited for applications requiring evaluation against large category vocabularies. For instance, when evaluating on LVIS with 1,203 categories, traditional fusion methods must perform separate forward passes for each category, while WeDetect computes visual features once and performs fast similarity matching.

## Data Curation and Training Strategy

A critical component of WeDetect's success is its massive, carefully curated training dataset. The researchers assembled 15 million images from diverse sources including SAM-1B, LAION, CC12M, and various object detection datasets. The key innovation lies in their automatic annotation pipeline that generates high-quality, multi-granularity labels for each detected object.

The annotation process uses an objectness detector to identify potential objects, followed by a fine-tuned multimodal large language model (Qwen2.5-VL 7B) that generates hierarchical labels. For example, an object might receive labels at multiple granularities: "animal," "dog," and "a yellow dog." This multi-granularity approach provides rich supervision that helps the model learn fine-grained vision-language alignment without relying on fusion layers.

The training follows a three-stage approach:

$$
\text{Stage 1: CLIP-style pretraining} \rightarrow \text{Stage 2: Head \& Neck training} \rightarrow \text{Stage 3: End-to-end finetuning}
$$

During training, labels are randomly sampled from each object's candidate list, creating diverse negative samples and enriching text variety. This strategy proves crucial for achieving strong open-vocabulary performance.

## WeDetect-Uni: Universal Object Proposals

Building upon the WeDetect foundation, WeDetect-Uni addresses the need for class-agnostic object proposals and introduces a new task called "object retrieval." The model is created by freezing the entire WeDetect detector and training only a single learnable objectness prompt, effectively repurposing the classification head for generic object detection.

![WeDetect-Uni Architecture](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12309v1/img-1.jpeg)
*Figure 2: WeDetect-Uni extends the base architecture by introducing a learnable objectness prompt while freezing the pretrained WeDetect parameters, enabling universal object proposal generation.*

The object retrieval capability represents a significant advancement over traditional image-level retrieval systems like CLIP. While CLIP can find images containing specific concepts, WeDetect-Uni can identify and retrieve images based on fine-grained local objects. The system pre-extracts object proposals and their embeddings, enabling fast retrieval through simple dot product operations between query embeddings and cached object features.

![Object Retrieval Example](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12309v1/img-4.jpeg)
*Figure 3: WeDetect-Uni's object retrieval capability allows users to search for specific objects within images, demonstrating fine-grained local perception beyond traditional image-level retrieval.*

## WeDetect-Ref: LLM-Based Referring Expression Comprehension

WeDetect-Ref tackles referring expression comprehension (REC) by reformulating it as a retrieval problem within a large language model framework. Traditional LLMs struggle with REC due to poor bounding box regression capabilities and slow sequential decoding. WeDetect-Ref overcomes these limitations by treating REC as object classification rather than coordinate prediction.

![WeDetect-Ref Architecture](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12309v1/img-2.jpeg)
*Figure 4: WeDetect-Ref processes object proposals in parallel through a binary classification head, avoiding the computational overhead of sequential token generation typical in LLMs.*

The process begins with WeDetect-Uni generating object proposals. Multi-scale RoI features are extracted and compressed into single "object tokens" through a linear projector. The LLM (based on Qwen3-VL) processes the full image, user query, and all object tokens simultaneously. A binary classification head determines which objects match the referring expression, enabling parallel processing rather than sequential generation.

The training involves three stages: region projector training with caption data, region perception fine-tuning with instruction data, and region classification training with detection datasets. This approach achieves remarkable efficiency gains—WeDetect-Ref operates 13× faster than the base Qwen3-VL model while achieving superior accuracy.

## Performance Results and Analysis

WeDetect demonstrates exceptional performance across multiple benchmarks while maintaining superior inference speeds. The base WeDetect model achieves state-of-the-art results on LVIS, COCO, and ODinW datasets. Notably, WeDetect-Large achieves 49.4 AP on LVIS, outperforming previous methods by significant margins while running 3× faster than comparable fusion-based models.

![Detection Results](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12309v1/img-5.jpeg)
*Figure 5: WeDetect achieves comprehensive object detection across diverse scenes with fine-grained category recognition and precise localization.*

WeDetect-Uni excels in universal proposal generation and object retrieval tasks. The model achieves high recall rates on standard benchmarks and demonstrates superior performance in the proposed object retrieval task, significantly outperforming image-level CLIP baselines with a 37.2 point F1 score improvement.

WeDetect-Ref sets new benchmarks for referring expression comprehension, achieving 93.2 average score on RefCOCO/+/g datasets while operating at 5.3 fps compared to 0.4 fps for traditional LLM approaches. The model also becomes the first LMM to exceed 50 AP on COCO detection (50.0 AP), demonstrating its versatility across different visual understanding tasks.

![Universal Proposals](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12309v1/img-6.jpeg)
*Figure 6: WeDetect-Uni generates comprehensive object proposals across diverse scenes, providing the foundation for various downstream applications including object retrieval and referring expression comprehension.*

## Unique Contributions and Innovations

WeDetect's primary contribution lies in demonstrating that retrieval-based methods can match or exceed the performance of computationally intensive fusion approaches while maintaining real-time inference speeds. This challenges the prevailing assumption that deep cross-modal fusion is necessary for high-accuracy open-vocabulary detection.

The introduction of object retrieval as a new task addresses a significant gap in fine-grained visual search capabilities. Unlike image-level retrieval systems, WeDetect-Uni enables users to search for specific objects within images, opening new possibilities for detailed visual exploration and verification.

The reformulation of referring expression comprehension as a retrieval problem within LLMs represents a paradigm shift that overcomes fundamental limitations of traditional language model approaches to visual localization. By avoiding bounding box regression and sequential decoding, WeDetect-Ref achieves both higher accuracy and dramatically improved efficiency.

## Technical Innovations and Implementation Details

The automatic annotation pipeline represents a significant technical achievement, combining objectness detection with fine-tuned multimodal language models to generate high-quality, hierarchical labels at scale. The multi-granularity labeling strategy proves crucial for training effective dual-tower models without fusion layers.

The three-stage training methodology carefully balances the preservation of pretrained knowledge with task-specific adaptation. The staged approach prevents disruption of valuable CLIP-style representations while enabling effective region-level learning.

For WeDetect-Ref, the parallel object processing mechanism through binary classification heads represents a fundamental departure from sequential LLM generation, enabling significant speedups while maintaining the language understanding capabilities of large models.

![REC Results](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12309v1/img-9.jpeg)
*Figure 7: WeDetect-Ref demonstrates precise referring expression comprehension, accurately identifying objects based on complex natural language descriptions.*

## Broader Impact and Significance

WeDetect's retrieval-based approach has implications beyond object detection, potentially influencing the design of future vision-language models. The demonstration that efficiency and accuracy are not mutually exclusive challenges existing architectural assumptions and may inspire new approaches to multimodal learning.

The real-time performance capabilities make advanced open-vocabulary detection practical for applications previously limited by computational constraints, including autonomous systems, augmented reality, and real-time content analysis. The unified framework spanning detection, proposal generation, and referring expression comprehension provides a comprehensive foundation for diverse visual understanding applications.

The introduction of object retrieval as a new capability addresses practical needs in visual search and content analysis, enabling more granular and precise visual query systems than previously possible with image-level approaches.

abstract: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to detect arbitrary classes via text prompts. Methods without cross-modal fusion layers (non-fusion) offer faster inference by treating recognition as a retrieval problem, \ie, matching regions to text queries in a shared embedding space. In this work, we fully explore this retrieval philosophy and demonstrate its unique advantages in efficiency and versatility through a model family named WeDetect: (1) State-of-the-art performance. WeDetect is a real-time detector with a dual-tower architecture. We show that, with well-curated data and full training, the non-fusion WeDetect surpasses other fusion models and establishes a strong open-vocabulary foundation. (2) Fast backtrack of historical data. WeDetect-Uni is a universal proposal generator based on WeDetect. We freeze the entire detector and only finetune an objectness prompt to retrieve generic object proposals across categories. Importantly, the proposal embeddings are class-specific and enable a new application, object retrieval, supporting retrieval objects in historical data. (3) Integration with LMMs for referring expression comprehension (REC). We further propose WeDetect-Ref, an LMM-based object classifier to handle complex referring expressions, which retrieves target objects from the proposal list extracted by WeDetect-Uni. It discards next-token prediction and classifies objects in a single forward pass. Together, the WeDetect family unifies detection, proposal generation, object retrieval, and REC under a coherent retrieval framework, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 15 benchmarks with high inference efficiency.

en.title: V-Rex: Real-Time Streaming Video LLM Acceleration via Dynamic KV Cache Retrieval
en.abstract:
Streaming video large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for real-time multimodal tasks such as video captioning, question answering, conversational agents, and augmented reality. However, these models face fundamental memory and computational challenges because their key-value (KV) caches grow substantially with continuous streaming video input. This process requires an iterative prefill stage, which is a unique feature of streaming video LLMs. Due to its iterative prefill stage, it suffers from significant limitations, including extensive computation, substantial data transfer, and degradation in accuracy. Crucially, this issue is exacerbated for edge deployment, which is the primary target for these models.
In this work, we propose V-Rex, the first software-hardware co-designed accelerator that comprehensively addresses both algorithmic and hardware bottlenecks in streaming video LLM inference. At its core, V-Rex introduces ReSV, a training-free dynamic KV cache retrieval algorithm. ReSV exploits temporal and spatial similarity-based token clustering to reduce excessive KV cache memory across video frames. To fully realize these algorithmic benefits, V-Rex offers a compact, low-latency hardware accelerator with a dynamic KV cache retrieval engine (DRE), featuring bit-level and early-exit based computing units. V-Rex achieves unprecedented real-time of 3.9-8.3 FPS and energy-efficient streaming video LLM inference on edge deployment with negligible accuracy loss. While DRE only accounts for 2.2% power and 2.0% area, the system delivers 1.9-19.7x speedup and 3.1-18.5x energy efficiency improvements over AGX Orin GPU. This work is the first to comprehensively tackle KV cache retrieval across algorithms and hardware, enabling real-time streaming video LLM inference on resource-constrained edge devices.

summary.summary: A software-hardware co-design, V-Rex, accelerates real-time streaming video Large Language Model inference by dynamically retrieving relevant Key-Value cache entries, particularly optimizing the iterative prefill stage. The system enables real-time frame rates (3.9-8.3 FPS) and reduces energy consumption by up to 12.8x on edge devices like the Jetson AGX Orin, while maintaining accuracy within a 0.8% drop.
originalProblem: Unbounded Key-Value (KV) cache growth in streaming video LLMs during the iterative prefill stage, rapidly exhausting GPU memory on resource-constrained edge devices.
Existing KV cache optimization methods were either destructive to contextual information or inefficient for the continuous, iterative nature of streaming video LLM prefill.
General-purpose GPUs struggle with the irregular and data-dependent computations of efficient KV cache retrieval algorithms, leading to high latency and energy consumption.
solution: A training-free, dynamic KV cache retrieval algorithm (ReSV) utilizing hash-bit key clustering for fast similarity grouping and WiCSum (Weighted Cumulative Sum) thresholding for adaptive token selection.

A compact, low-latency specialized hardware accelerator (DRE) with a Hash-bit Cluster Unit (HCU) and WiCSum Threshold Unit (WTU) to efficiently process irregular computations, and a KV Cache Management Unit (KVMU) for optimized hierarchical memory access.
A software-hardware co-design that tightly integrates the ReSV algorithm and DRE hardware to offload latency-critical, irregular tasks and manage memory effectively, enabling real-time operation.
keyInsights: The iterative prefill stage in streaming video LLMs necessitates specialized KV cache retrieval strategies that effectively leverage video's inherent temporal and spatial similarity.

Lightweight hash-bit clustering can significantly reduce the KV cache search space, while dynamic, layer- and head-adaptive token selection (WiCSum thresholding) is crucial for efficient resource utilization.
Offloading irregular and data-dependent KV cache management computations to specialized hardware is essential for overcoming GPU inefficiencies and achieving real-time performance on edge devices.
results: Achieved real-time streaming inference on edge devices (Jetson AGX Orin) with 3.9-8.3 FPS (2.2-7.3x speedup) and up to 12.8x higher energy efficiency for frame processing.

Maintained high accuracy with only a 0.8% average drop compared to the baseline, achieving this with a significantly low retrieval ratio (average 32.7% for frame processing, 2.5% for text generation).

The compact DRE hardware contributes minimally (2.0% chip area, 2.4% power) and enables robust memory management, allowing continuous operation beyond out-of-memory limits encountered by other accelerators.

en.overview:
## Software-Hardware Co-Design for Streaming Video LLMs

V-Rex introduces a comprehensive solution for one of the most pressing challenges in modern artificial intelligence: enabling real-time inference for streaming video Large Language Models (LLMs) on resource-constrained edge devices. The paper presents the first software-hardware co-designed accelerator that addresses the fundamental bottlenecks in streaming video LLM inference through integrated algorithmic and hardware innovations.

![V-Rex Overview](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-0.jpeg)
*Figure 1: V-Rex system overview showing the software-level ReSV algorithm and hardware-level acceleration components including KV Cache Prediction Unit (KVPU) and KV Cache Management Unit (KVMU).*

The core challenge lies in the explosive growth of Key-Value (KV) caches during the iterative prefill stage unique to streaming video LLMs. Unlike traditional text-based LLMs that primarily operate in a generation stage, streaming video LLMs must continuously process incoming video frames, leading to unbounded KV cache growth that quickly exhausts available GPU memory. This makes real-time inference impractical, particularly for edge deployment where memory and computational resources are severely limited.

## The Streaming Video LLM Challenge

Streaming video LLMs differ fundamentally from their offline counterparts in their operational characteristics. These models must process continuous real-time video inputs while maintaining conversational context across multiple queries, requiring a unique two-stage inference pattern.

![Streaming Video LLM Process](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-1.jpeg)
*Figure 2: Example of streaming video LLM processing showing how frames are continuously processed while maintaining conversational context.*

The iterative prefill stage dominates the computational workload, where each incoming video frame is processed sequentially through the vision tower and transformer layers, with KV caches growing linearly over time. This differs significantly from traditional text LLMs where the prefill stage occurs once at the beginning, followed by autoregressive generation.

![KV Cache Growth](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-2.jpeg)
*Figure 3: Illustration of the iterative prefill stage in streaming video LLMs, showing how KV caches accumulate across multiple frames before question processing.*

The memory footprint analysis reveals that KV caches can consume up to 140 GB for a 40-minute video, far exceeding typical edge GPU memory capacity of 32 GB. This creates a fundamental scalability barrier where systems run out of memory within minutes of operation.

![Memory Analysis](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-3.jpeg)
*Figure 4: Memory footprint analysis showing KV cache growth over video duration and the resulting prefill overhead dominance in streaming scenarios.*

## ReSV: Dynamic KV Cache Retrieval Algorithm

The software component of V-Rex is the Real-Time Streaming Video LLM retrieval Algorithm (ReSV), a training-free solution that exploits the temporal and spatial similarity inherent in video data to dramatically reduce memory requirements while preserving accuracy.

ReSV operates through two key innovations: hash-bit key clustering and weighted cumulative sum thresholding. The hash-bit clustering mechanism reduces the dimensionality of key representations using random hyperplane projections, creating compact binary signatures that enable efficient similarity detection through Hamming distance computation.

The process begins with hash-bit generation, where key matrices undergo dimensionality reduction to create ultra-compact representations (≤0.5% of original dimension). These hash-bits are then compared using Hamming distance to identify similar tokens across video frames, leveraging the high temporal correlation in video content.

![Hash-bit Generation](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-9.jpeg)
*Figure 5: Hash-bit generation process using hyperplane multiplication to create compact binary representations of key vectors.*

The clustering process groups similar tokens based on Hamming distance thresholds, creating representative clusters that significantly reduce the computational overhead of similarity detection compared to high-dimensional cosine similarity calculations.

![Hamming Distance Clustering](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-10.jpeg)
*Figure 6: Hamming distance clustering process showing how tokens are grouped based on binary hash-bit similarity.*

The second innovation is the Weighted Cumulative Sum (WiCSum) thresholding mechanism, which dynamically determines the optimal number of tokens to retrieve for each transformer layer and attention head. Unlike fixed top-k selection strategies, WiCSum adapts to varying importance distributions across different model components.

![WiCSum Thresholding](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-12.jpeg)
*Figure 7: WiCSum thresholding process showing dynamic token selection based on weighted cumulative scores with early exit capability.*

The algorithm computes relevance scores between queries and cluster representatives, then applies a threshold-based selection with early exit optimization. This approach ensures that only the most critical tokens are retrieved while avoiding the inefficiencies of fixed selection policies.

## Hardware Acceleration Architecture

The hardware component consists of the Dynamic KV Cache Retrieval Engine (DRE), designed to efficiently accelerate the irregular, data-dependent operations of ReSV while managing the complex memory hierarchy required for large-scale KV cache storage.

![Hardware Architecture](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-13.jpeg)
*Figure 8: V-Rex hardware architecture showing the LLM Execution Engine (LXE) and Dynamic KV Cache Retrieval Engine (DRE) components.*

The DRE comprises two specialized units: the KV Cache Prediction Unit (KVPU) and the KV Cache Management Unit (KVMU). The KVPU handles the computationally intensive clustering and thresholding operations through dedicated hardware units optimized for the specific computational patterns of ReSV.

The Hash-bit Cluster Unit (HCU) performs parallel Hamming distance computations using custom XOR accumulator arrays, while the WiCSum Threshold Unit (WTU) implements early-exit bucket sorting to minimize computational overhead during dynamic token selection.

![Early Exit Sorting](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-14.jpeg)
*Figure 9: Early exit sorting mechanism in the WTU showing how threshold-based termination reduces computational requirements.*

The KVMU manages the hierarchical memory system, implementing cluster-based memory mapping to optimize data locality and minimize PCIe transfer overhead. This design enables efficient batching of memory accesses while hiding retrieval latencies through pipelining with the main computation.

## Experimental Results and Performance Analysis

V-Rex demonstrates substantial performance improvements across edge and server deployments. On the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge platform, V-Rex achieves real-time streaming inference (≥2 FPS) with 2.2-7.3× speedup over GPU baselines and 5.5-10.2× energy efficiency improvements.

![Performance Results](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-16.jpeg)
*Figure 10: Performance comparison showing latency and energy efficiency improvements across different batch sizes and sequence lengths on both edge and server platforms.*

The results show that V-Rex maintains consistent performance even at longer sequence lengths where baseline GPU methods fail due to memory limitations. The end-to-end latency analysis reveals up to 5.4× reduction compared to conventional approaches.

![End-to-End Latency](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-17.jpeg)
*Figure 11: End-to-end latency breakdown showing how V-Rex reduces prefill overhead across different sequence lengths.*

Accuracy evaluation on the COIN benchmark demonstrates that ReSV maintains high accuracy with only 0.8% average degradation while achieving the lowest retrieval ratio (32.7% for frame processing) among all comparison methods. This efficiency stems from the dynamic selection mechanism that adapts to varying token importance across model layers and attention heads.

![Accuracy Analysis](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-22.jpeg)
*Figure 12: Accuracy comparison and retrieval efficiency showing ReSV's superior performance with minimal accuracy loss.*

The ablation study confirms that the software-hardware co-design is essential for achieving optimal performance. While software optimizations alone provide 2.8× speedup, the complete system achieves 8.1× speedup with 10.2× energy reduction, demonstrating the critical importance of specialized hardware acceleration.

## Implications and Future Directions

V-Rex represents a significant advancement in making streaming video LLMs practical for real-world deployment, particularly in resource-constrained edge environments. The work demonstrates that intelligent software-hardware co-design can overcome fundamental scaling barriers that have historically limited the deployment of sophisticated multimodal AI systems.

The training-free nature of ReSV and the modular design of the DRE hardware make the approach highly adaptable to different streaming video LLM architectures and deployment scenarios. The minimal hardware overhead (2.0% chip area, 2.4% power) ensures that the benefits can be integrated into existing AI accelerator designs without significant cost increases.

This research opens new avenues for real-time multimodal AI applications including augmented reality systems, intelligent robotics, and interactive video understanding platforms. The ability to process long-context video streams efficiently while maintaining conversational coherence enables new classes of applications that were previously impractical due to system limitations.

The work also highlights the importance of domain-specific optimization for emerging AI workloads. As multimodal models become increasingly important, the lessons from V-Rex regarding the need for specialized algorithms and hardware designs tailored to specific computational patterns will likely influence future accelerator development across the broader AI hardware landscape.

zh.title: V-Rex: 通过动态KV缓存检索实现实时流式视频大语言模型加速
zh.abstract:
流媒体视频大语言模型（LLM）正日益被用于实时多模态任务，例如视频字幕、问答、对话代理和增强现实。然而，这些模型面临着基本的内存和计算挑战，因为它们的键值（KV）缓存在连续流媒体视频输入下会显著增长。这一过程需要一个迭代预填充阶段，这是流媒体视频LLM的一个独特特性。由于其迭代预填充阶段，模型存在显著局限性，包括计算量大、数据传输多以及精度下降。更重要的是，这个问题在边缘部署中尤为突出，而边缘部署正是这些模型的主要目标场景。

在这项工作中，我们提出了V-Rex，这是首个软硬件协同设计的加速器，它全面解决了流媒体视频LLM推理中的算法和硬件瓶颈。V-Rex的核心是引入了ReSV，一种免训练的动态KV缓存检索算法。ReSV利用基于时空相似性的token聚类来减少跨视频帧过多的KV缓存内存。为了充分发挥这些算法优势，V-Rex提供了一个紧凑、低延迟的硬件加速器，其中包含一个动态KV缓存检索引擎（DRE），该引擎具有位级和提前退出计算单元。V-Rex在边缘部署上实现了前所未有的3.9-8.3 FPS实时性和高能效的流媒体视频LLM推理，且精度损失可忽略不计。尽管DRE仅占2.2%的功耗和2.0%的面积，但该系统在AGX Orin GPU的基础上，实现了1.9-19.7倍的加速和3.1-18.5倍的能效提升。这项工作首次从算法和硬件层面全面解决了KV缓存检索问题，使得在资源受限的边缘设备上进行实时流媒体视频LLM推理成为可能。

summary.summary: V-Rex 是一种软硬件协同设计，它通过动态检索相关的键值缓存条目来加速实时流媒体视频大型语言模型推理，特别是优化了迭代预填充阶段。该系统在 Jetson AGX Orin 等边缘设备上实现了实时帧率（3.9-8.3 FPS），并将能耗降低了高达 12.8 倍，同时保持准确性下降在 0.8% 以内。
originalProblem: 在流媒体视频大型语言模型的迭代预填充阶段，键值（KV）缓存的无限制增长，迅速耗尽资源受限边缘设备上的 GPU 内存。
现有的 KV 缓存优化方法要么破坏了上下文信息，要么对于流媒体视频大型语言模型预填充的连续迭代特性而言效率低下。
通用 GPU 难以处理高效 KV 缓存检索算法中不规则和数据相关的计算，导致高延迟和高能耗。
solution: 一种无需训练的动态 KV 缓存检索算法（ReSV），利用哈希位键聚类实现快速相似性分组，并采用 WiCSum（加权累积和）阈值处理进行自适应令牌选择。
一种紧凑、低延迟的专用硬件加速器（DRE），包含哈希位聚类单元（HCU）和 WiCSum 阈值单元（WTU），用于高效处理不规则计算，以及一个 KV 缓存管理单元（KVMU），用于优化分层内存访问。
一种软硬件协同设计，紧密集成 ReSV 算法和 DRE 硬件，以卸载延迟敏感的、不规则的任务并有效管理内存，从而实现实时操作。
keyInsights: 流媒体视频大型语言模型中的迭代预填充阶段需要专门的 KV 缓存检索策略，以有效利用视频固有的时间和空间相似性。
轻量级哈希位聚类可以显著缩小 KV 缓存搜索空间，而动态的、层和头部自适应的令牌选择（WiCSum 阈值处理）对于高效的资源利用至关重要。
将不规则和数据相关的 KV 缓存管理计算卸载到专用硬件对于克服 GPU 效率低下并在边缘设备上实现实时性能至关重要。
results: 在边缘设备（Jetson AGX Orin）上实现了实时流媒体推理，帧率达到 3.9-8.3 FPS（2.2-7.3 倍加速），帧处理能效提高了高达 12.8 倍。
与基线相比，仅有 0.8% 的平均准确率下降，同时实现了极低的检索率（帧处理平均 32.7%，文本生成平均 2.5%）。
紧凑的 DRE 硬件贡献极小（2.0% 的芯片面积，2.4% 的功耗），并实现了强大的内存管理，允许在其他加速器遇到的内存不足限制之外持续运行。

zh.overview:
## 专用于流媒体视频大语言模型的软硬件协同设计

V-Rex 为现代人工智能领域最紧迫的挑战之一——在资源受限的边缘设备上实现流媒体视频大语言模型（LLM）的实时推理——引入了一套全面的解决方案。该论文提出了第一个软硬件协同设计的加速器，通过集成的算法和硬件创新，解决了流媒体视频大语言模型推理中的根本瓶颈。

![V-Rex Overview](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-0.jpeg)
*图1：V-Rex 系统概览，展示了软件层的ReSV算法和硬件层的加速组件，包括键值缓存预测单元（KVPU）和键值缓存管理单元（KVMU）。*

核心挑战在于流媒体视频大语言模型特有的迭代预填充阶段中键值（KV）缓存的爆炸式增长。与主要在生成阶段运行的传统文本大语言模型不同，流媒体视频大语言模型必须持续处理传入的视频帧，导致KV缓存无限增长，迅速耗尽可用的GPU内存。这使得实时推理变得不切实际，尤其是在内存和计算资源严重受限的边缘部署中。

## 流媒体视频大语言模型的挑战

流媒体视频大语言模型在操作特性上与其离线对应模型有根本区别。这些模型必须处理连续的实时视频输入，同时在多个查询中保持对话上下文，这需要独特的两阶段推理模式。

![Streaming Video LLM Process](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-1.jpeg)
*图2：流媒体视频大语言模型处理示例，展示了如何持续处理帧同时保持对话上下文。*

迭代预填充阶段占据了主要的计算工作负载，其中每个传入的视频帧通过视觉塔和变换器层按序处理，KV缓存随时间线性增长。这与传统文本大语言模型显著不同，传统文本大语言模型的预填充阶段只在开始时发生一次，随后是自回归生成。

![KV Cache Growth](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-2.jpeg)
*图3：流媒体视频大语言模型中迭代预填充阶段的图示，显示了在问题处理之前KV缓存如何跨多个帧累积。*

内存占用分析显示，40分钟的视频，KV缓存可以消耗高达140 GB，远超典型边缘GPU 32 GB的内存容量。这造成了一个根本性的可扩展性障碍，系统在运行几分钟内就会耗尽内存。

![Memory Analysis](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-3.jpeg)
*图4：内存占用分析，显示了KV缓存随视频时长而增长，以及在流媒体场景中由此导致的预填充开销主导地位。*

## ReSV：动态KV缓存检索算法

V-Rex 的软件组件是实时流媒体视频大语言模型检索算法（ReSV），这是一种无需训练的解决方案，它利用视频数据固有的时间和空间相似性，在保持准确性的同时大幅减少内存需求。

ReSV 通过两项关键创新运行：哈希位键聚类和加权累积和阈值。哈希位聚类机制使用随机超平面投影降低键表示的维度，创建紧凑的二进制签名，从而通过汉明距离计算实现高效的相似性检测。

该过程从哈希位生成开始，其中键矩阵经过降维处理，以创建超紧凑表示（原始维度的≤0.5%）。然后，这些哈希位使用汉明距离进行比较，以识别视频帧中相似的标记，从而利用视频内容中高度的时间相关性。

![Hash-bit Generation](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-9.jpeg)
*图5：使用超平面乘法生成哈希位以创建键向量的紧凑二进制表示的过程。*

聚类过程根据汉明距离阈值对相似令牌进行分组，创建代表性簇，与高维余弦相似度计算相比，这显著降低了相似度检测的计算开销。

![Hamming Distance Clustering](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-10.jpeg)
*图6：汉明距离聚类过程，展示了如何根据二进制哈希位相似性对令牌进行分组。*

第二个创新是加权累积和（WiCSum）阈值机制，它动态确定每个Transformer层和注意力头要检索的最佳令牌数量。与固定的top-k选择策略不同，WiCSum适应不同模型组件中变化的重要性分布。

![WiCSum Thresholding](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-12.jpeg)
*图7：WiCSum阈值处理过程，展示了基于加权累积分数的动态令牌选择，并具有提前退出能力。*

该算法计算查询和簇代表之间的相关性分数，然后应用基于阈值的选择并进行提前退出优化。这种方法确保只检索最关键的令牌，同时避免了固定选择策略的低效率。

## 硬件加速架构

硬件组件包括动态KV缓存检索引擎（DRE），该引擎旨在有效加速ReSV中不规则、数据依赖的操作，同时管理大规模KV缓存存储所需的复杂内存层次结构。

![Hardware Architecture](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-13.jpeg)
*图8：V-Rex硬件架构，展示了LLM执行引擎（LXE）和动态KV缓存检索引擎（DRE）组件。*

DRE包含两个专用单元：KV缓存预测单元（KVPU）和KV缓存管理单元（KVMU）。KVPU通过专用的硬件单元处理计算密集型聚类和阈值操作，这些单元针对ReSV的特定计算模式进行了优化。

哈希位簇单元（HCU）使用自定义XOR累加器阵列执行并行汉明距离计算，而WiCSum阈值单元（WTU）则实现提前退出桶排序，以最小化动态令牌选择期间的计算开销。

![Early Exit Sorting](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-14.jpeg)
*图9：WTU中的提前退出排序机制，展示了基于阈值的终止如何减少计算需求。*

KVMU管理分层内存系统，实现了基于簇的内存映射以优化数据局部性并最小化PCIe传输开销。这种设计能够实现高效的内存访问批处理，同时通过与主计算的流水线操作来隐藏检索延迟。

## 实验结果与性能分析

V-Rex在边缘和服务器部署中展示了显著的性能提升。在NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin边缘平台上，V-Rex实现了实时流式推理（≥2 FPS），相较于GPU基线，速度提升了2.2-7.3倍，并且能效提升了5.5-10.2倍。

![Performance Results](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-16.jpeg)
*图10：性能比较，展示了在边缘和服务器平台，不同批次大小和序列长度下的延迟和能效提升。*

结果表明，V-Rex即使在基线GPU方法因内存限制而失效的较长序列长度下，也能保持一致的性能。端到端延迟分析显示，与传统方法相比，延迟减少高达5.4倍。

![端到端延迟](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-17.jpeg)
*图11：端到端延迟分解，显示V-Rex如何降低不同序列长度的预填充开销。*

对COIN基准的准确性评估表明，ReSV在实现所有比较方法中最低检索率（帧处理为32.7%）的同时，仍保持高准确性，平均降级仅为0.8%。这种效率源于动态选择机制，该机制能适应模型层和注意力头中不同的token重要性。

![准确性分析](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.12284v1/img-22.jpeg)
*图12：准确性比较和检索效率，显示ReSV在最小精度损失下的卓越性能。*

消融研究证实，软硬件协同设计对于实现最佳性能至关重要。虽然仅软件优化就能提供2.8倍的加速，但完整系统实现了8.1倍的加速和10.2倍的能耗降低，这表明专用硬件加速的关键重要性。

## 影响与未来方向

V-Rex代表了使流媒体视频LLM在实际部署中，特别是在资源受限的边缘环境中变得实用的重大进步。这项工作表明，智能的软硬件协同设计可以克服历史上限制复杂多模态AI系统部署的基本扩展障碍。

ReSV的免训练特性和DRE硬件的模块化设计使该方法高度适应不同的流媒体视频LLM架构和部署场景。最小的硬件开销（2.0%芯片面积，2.4%功耗）确保了这些优势可以集成到现有AI加速器设计中，而不会显著增加成本。

这项研究为实时多模态AI应用开辟了新途径，包括增强现实系统、智能机器人和交互式视频理解平台。高效处理长上下文视频流并保持对话连贯性的能力，使得以前由于系统限制而无法实现的新型应用成为可能。

这项工作还强调了针对新兴AI工作负载进行领域特定优化的重要性。随着多模态模型变得越来越重要，V-Rex关于需要根据特定计算模式定制专用算法和硬件设计的经验教训，可能会影响未来更广泛AI硬件领域的加速器开发。

abstract:
Streaming video large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for real-time multimodal tasks such as video captioning, question answering, conversational agents, and augmented reality. However, these models face fundamental memory and computational challenges because their key-value (KV) caches grow substantially with continuous streaming video input. This process requires an iterative prefill stage, which is a unique feature of streaming video LLMs. Due to its iterative prefill stage, it suffers from significant limitations, including extensive computation, substantial data transfer, and degradation in accuracy. Crucially, this issue is exacerbated for edge deployment, which is the primary target for these models.
  In this work, we propose V-Rex, the first software-hardware co-designed accelerator that comprehensively addresses both algorithmic and hardware bottlenecks in streaming video LLM inference. At its core, V-Rex introduces ReSV, a training-free dynamic KV cache retrieval algorithm. ReSV exploits temporal and spatial similarity-based token clustering to reduce excessive KV cache memory across video frames. To fully realize these algorithmic benefits, V-Rex offers a compact, low-latency hardware accelerator with a dynamic KV cache retrieval engine (DRE), featuring bit-level and early-exit based computing units. V-Rex achieves unprecedented real-time of 3.9-8.3 FPS and energy-efficient streaming video LLM inference on edge deployment with negligible accuracy loss. While DRE only accounts for 2.2% power and 2.0% area, the system delivers 1.9-19.7x speedup and 3.1-18.5x energy efficiency improvements over AGX Orin GPU. This work is the first to comprehensively tackle KV cache retrieval across algorithms and hardware, enabling real-time streaming video LLM inference on resource-constrained edge devices.
title: V-Rex: Real-Time Streaming Video LLM Acceleration via Dynamic KV Cache Retrieval

V-Rex: Real-Time Streaming Video LLM Acceleration via Dynamic KV Cache Retrieval Streaming video large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for real-time multimodal tasks such as video captioning, question answering, conversational agents, and augmented reality. However, these models face fundamental memory and computational challenges because their key-value (KV) caches grow substantially with continuous streaming video input. This process requires an iterative prefill stage, which is a unique feature of streaming video LLMs. Due to its iterative prefill stage, it suffers from significant limitations, including extensive computation, substantial data transfer, and degradation in accuracy. Crucially, this issue is exacerbated for edge deployment, which is the primary target for these models.
  In this work, we propose V-Rex, the first software-hardware co-designed accelerator that comprehensively addresses both algorithmic and hardware bottlenecks in streaming video LLM inference. At its core, V-Rex introduces ReSV, a training-free dynamic KV cache retrieval algorithm. ReSV exploits temporal and spatial similarity-based token clustering to reduce excessive KV cache memory across video frames. To fully realize these algorithmic benefits, V-Rex offers a compact, low-latency hardware accelerator with a dynamic KV cache retrieval engine (DRE), featuring bit-level and early-exit based computing units. V-Rex achieves unprecedented real-time of 3.9-8.3 FPS and energy-efficient streaming video LLM inference on edge deployment with negligible accuracy loss. While DRE only accounts for 2.2% power and 2.0% area, the system delivers 1.9-19.7x speedup and 3.1-18.5x energy efficiency improvements over AGX Orin GPU. This work is the first to comprehensively tackle KV cache retrieval across algorithms and hardware, enabling real-time streaming video LLM inference on resource-constrained edge devices.

abstract: Conversational search systems increasingly provide source citations, yet how citation or source presentation formats influence user engagement remains unclear. We conducted a crowdsourcing user experiment with 394 participants comparing four source presentation designs that varied citation visibility and accessibility: collapsible lists, hover cards, footer lists, and aligned sidebars.High-visibility interfaces generated substantially more hovering on sources, though clicking remained infrequent across all conditions. While interface design showed limited effects on user experience and perception measures, it significantly influenced knowledge, interest, and agreement changes. High-visibility interfaces initially reduced knowledge gain and interest, but these positive effects emerged with increasing source usage. The sidebar condition uniquely increased agreement change. Our findings demonstrate that source presentation alone may not enhance engagement and can even reduce it when insufficient sources are provided.
title: Not All Transparency Is Equal: Source Presentation Effects on Attention, Interaction, and Persuasion in Conversational Search

abstract: Large language models have become essential tools for code comprehension, enabling developers to query unfamiliar codebases through natural language interfaces. However, LLM hallucination, generating plausible but factually incorrect citations to source code, remains a critical barrier to reliable developer assistance. This paper addresses the challenges of achieving verifiable, citation grounded code comprehension through hybrid retrieval and lightweight structural reasoning. Our work is grounded in systematic evaluation across 30 Python repositories with 180 developer queries, comparing retrieval modalities, graph expansion strategies, and citation verification mechanisms. We find that challenges of citation accuracy arise from the interplay between sparse lexical matching, dense semantic similarity, and cross file architectural dependencies. Among these, cross file evidence discovery is the largest contributor to citation completeness, but it is largely overlooked because existing systems rely on pure textual similarity without leveraging code structure. We advocate for citation grounded generation as an architectural principle for code comprehension systems and demonstrate this need by achieving 92 percent citation accuracy with zero hallucinations. Specifically, we develop a hybrid retrieval system combining BM25 sparse matching, BGE dense embeddings, and Neo4j graph expansion via import relationships, which outperforms single mode baselines by 14 to 18 percentage points while discovering cross file evidence missed by pure text similarity in 62 percent of architectural queries.

abstract: Existing Text-to-SQL benchmarks primarily focus on single-table queries or limited joins in general-purpose domains, and thus fail to reflect the complexity of domain-specific, multi-table and geospatial reasoning, To address this limitation, we introduce FLOODSQL-BENCH, a geospatially grounded benchmark for the flood management domain that integrates heterogeneous datasets through key-based, spatial, and hybrid joins. The benchmark captures realistic flood-related information needs by combining social, infrastructural, and hazard data layers. We systematically evaluate recent large language models with the same retrieval-augmented generation settings and measure their performance across difficulty tiers. By providing a unified, open benchmark grounded in real-world disaster management data, FLOODSQL-BENCH establishes a practical testbed for advancing Text-to-SQL research in high-stakes application domains.
title: FloodSQL-Bench: A Retrieval-Augmented Benchmark for Geospatially-Grounded Text-to-SQL

abstract: Whole-slide multiplex imaging of brain tissue generates massive information-dense images that are challenging to analyze and require custom software. We present an alternative query-driven programming-free strategy using a multiplex visual search engine (mViSE) that learns the multifaceted brain tissue chemoarchitecture, cytoarchitecture, and myeloarchitecture. Our divide-and-conquer strategy organizes the data into panels of related molecular markers and uses self-supervised learning to train a multiplex encoder for each panel with explicit visual confirmation of successful learning. Multiple panels can be combined to process visual queries for retrieving similar communities of individual cells or multicellular niches using information-theoretic methods. The retrievals can be used for diverse purposes including tissue exploration, delineating brain regions and cortical cell layers, profiling and comparing brain regions without computer programming. We validated mViSE's ability to retrieve single cells, proximal cell pairs, tissue patches, delineate cortical layers, brain regions and sub-regions. mViSE is provided as an open-source QuPath plug-in.

abstract: While end-to-end encryption protects the content of messages, it does not secure metadata, which exposes sender and receiver information through traffic analysis. A plausible approach to protecting this metadata is to have senders post encrypted messages on a public bulletin board and receivers scan it for relevant messages. Oblivious message retrieval (OMR) leverages homomorphic encryption (HE) to improve user experience in this solution by delegating the scan to a resource-rich server while preserving privacy. A key process in OMR is the homomorphic detection of pertinent messages for the receiver from the bulletin board. It relies on a specialized matrix-vector multiplication algorithm, which involves extensive multiplications between ciphertext vectors and plaintext matrices, as well as homomorphic rotations. The computationally intensive nature of this process limits the practicality of OMR. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a hardware architecture to accelerate the matrix-vector multiplication algorithm. The building homomorphic operators in this algorithm are implemented using high-level synthesis, with design parameters for different parallelism levels. These operators are then deployed on a field-programmable gate array platform using an efficient design space exploration strategy to accelerate homomorphic matrix-vector multiplication. Compared to a software implementation, the proposed hardware accelerator achieves a 13.86x speedup.
title: Leveraging FPGAs for Homomorphic Matrix-Vector Multiplication in Oblivious Message Retrieval

en.title: Automating Historical Insight Extraction from Large-Scale Newspaper Archives via Neural Topic Modeling
en.abstract: Extracting coherent and human-understandable themes from large collections of unstructured historical newspaper archives presents significant challenges due to topic evolution, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) noise, and the sheer volume of text. Traditional topic-modeling methods, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), often fall short in capturing the complexity and dynamic nature of discourse in historical texts. To address these limitations, we employ BERTopic. This neural topic-modeling approach leverages transformerbased embeddings to extract and classify topics, which, despite its growing popularity, still remains underused in historical research. Our study focuses on articles published between 1955 and 2018, specifically examining discourse on nuclear power and nuclear safety. We analyze various topic distributions across the corpus and trace their temporal evolution to uncover long-term trends and shifts in public discourse. This enables us to more accurately explore patterns in public discourse, including the co-occurrence of themes related to nuclear power and nuclear weapons and their shifts in topic importance over time. Our study demonstrates the scalability and contextual sensitivity of BERTopic as an alternative to traditional approaches, offering richer insights into historical discourses extracted from newspaper archives. These findings contribute to historical, nuclear, and social-science research while reflecting on current limitations and proposing potential directions for future work.

summary.summary: Researchers at the University of Luxembourg developed a neural topic modeling framework, BERTopic, to automatically extract and trace coherent historical themes from large digitized newspaper archives. This method consistently surpassed classical topic models in topic coherence and diversity, effectively illustrating the temporal evolution of public discourse surrounding significant events such as nuclear accidents.
originalProblem: Traditional topic models (e.g., LDA, NMF) exhibit limitations in capturing complex, dynamic discourse and deep semantic relationships within historical texts, often producing generic themes.
Manual analysis of vast, unstructured historical newspaper archives is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and struggles with scalability and objectivity when identifying long-term trends.
Existing computational methods are often sensitive to linguistic variations, inherent biases, and OCR noise prevalent in digitized historical documents.
solution: Implemented BERTopic, a neural topic modeling framework that leverages transformer-based embeddings (GTE and Jina) and hierarchical clustering (UMAP, HDBSCAN) for context-sensitive document representation.
Extended BERTopic with temporal metadata to enable dynamic topic modeling, allowing the tracking and visualization of topic evolution over specific historical periods.
Conducted comprehensive data preprocessing, including multi-language translation to English, linguistic cleaning, and optimization, on a large corpus of over 148,000 historical newspaper articles.
keyInsights: Neural topic models, particularly BERTopic with transformer embeddings, are substantially more effective for historical text analysis than classical models, as they capture richer semantic context and produce more coherent topics.
The quality and contextual capabilities of the embedding model are crucial for robust topic coherence and diversity, often being more impactful than the model's sheer size.
Dynamic topic modeling with BERTopic effectively reveals shifts in public discourse over time, enabling the identification of discussion spikes corresponding to major historical events.
results: BERTopic consistently outperformed classical LDA and NMF models across quantitative metrics, showing superior topic coherence and diversity, alongside improved computational efficiency.

Dynamic topic analysis successfully identified and visualized clear surges in public discourse related to historical events like the Harrisburg accident (1979), Chernobyl disaster (1986), and Fukushima crisis (2011).
The framework processed a large corpus of over 148,000 articles published between 1955 and 2018, demonstrating strong scalability and robustness for complex historical datasets.

en.overview:
## Overview

This research presents a comprehensive study applying neural topic modeling to automatically extract historical insights from large-scale digitized newspaper archives. The work addresses fundamental limitations of traditional text analysis methods when dealing with vast collections of historical documents, demonstrating how modern neural approaches can provide more nuanced and temporally aware analysis of public discourse evolution.

![Methodology Overview](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.11635v1/img-0.jpeg)
*Figure 1: Complete methodology workflow showing the stages from data collection through static and dynamic topic modeling, including preprocessing, embedding generation, and evaluation phases.*

## Problem and Motivation

Historical text analysis has traditionally relied on manual methods that, while providing deep contextual understanding, are inherently limited by scale and efficiency when confronting "big data" collections. Classical computational approaches like Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) offered some automation but suffered from significant drawbacks: they require predefined topic numbers, struggle with contextual nuances, are sensitive to OCR noise common in digitized historical documents, and rely on Bag-of-Words representations that fail to capture semantic relationships.

The research motivation centers on leveraging neural topic modeling, specifically BERTopic, to overcome these limitations. Neural approaches utilize transformer-based embeddings that generate contextualized representations, capturing semantic meaning based on context rather than simple word co-occurrence. This contextual sensitivity is crucial for understanding nuanced historical discourse and tracking how language and themes evolve over time.

## Dataset and Methodology

The study utilized a curated dataset from the "impresso: Media Monitoring of the Past" project, comprising over 148,000 digitized newspaper articles and advertisements published between 1955 and 2018. The corpus focused specifically on nuclear power and nuclear safety discourse, providing rich material for analyzing public opinion evolution around these critical topics.

The methodology involved several key stages:

**Data Preparation**: Documents were temporally segmented into four chronological periods (1955-1970, 1971-1986, 1987-2002, 2003-2018). Original texts in French, German, and Luxembourgish were translated to English using Google Translate. Comprehensive preprocessing included noise removal, linguistic processing with spaCy (stopword removal, tokenization, lemmatization), and filtering documents with fewer than 20 tokens.

**Neural Embeddings**: The approach utilized sentence transformer models, specifically 'gte-base-en-v1.5' and 'jina-embeddings-v2-base-en' from Hugging Face, chosen for their semantic relationship capture capabilities and ability to handle long sequences (up to 8,192 tokens).

**BERTopic Implementation**: The core methodology employed BERTopic, which combines transformer-based embeddings with hierarchical clustering. The process involves:
- UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) for dimensionality reduction while preserving local structure
- HDBSCAN (Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering) for clustering similar documents without requiring predefined cluster counts
- C-TF-IDF (Class-based Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency) for topic representation using representative words for each cluster

Both static topic modeling (for overall thematic analysis) and dynamic topic modeling (incorporating temporal metadata to track evolution) were implemented.

## Key Findings

The research demonstrated clear superiority of neural approaches over classical methods across multiple evaluation dimensions:

**Quantitative Performance**: BERTopic consistently outperformed classical methods (LDA, NMF, and their TF-IDF/NER variants) in topic coherence, topic diversity, and computational efficiency. The GTE embedding model showed particularly strong performance, while Jina embeddings provided comparable results despite being more compact.

**Hyperparameter Optimization**: Interestingly, hyperparameter optimization using Tree of Parzen Estimators (TPE) provided only modest improvements while requiring substantial computational resources (over 24 hours on GPU). This finding suggests that BERTopic's default configurations are robust and often sufficient, particularly under resource constraints.

**Embedding Model Differences**: Qualitative analysis revealed that different embedding models emphasize different thematic aspects. GTE embeddings focused more on technical, legal, and political dimensions, while Jina embeddings emphasized geopolitical and environmental concerns. This indicates that embedding choice can be tailored to specific research interests.

**Temporal Analysis Capabilities**: The dynamic modeling component proved particularly valuable, successfully identifying and visualizing discourse spikes around major historical events. The analysis captured:

$$
\text{Event Impact} = f(\text{Topic Frequency}, \text{Time}, \text{Historical Context})
$$

Notable events detected include the Harrisburg accident (1979), Chernobyl disaster (1986), Hiroshima 50th anniversary (1995), and Fukushima crisis (2011). Each showed distinct temporal patterns reflecting the nature and scale of public response.

## Technical Innovation

The research makes several technical contributions to the field of computational history:

**Contextual Embeddings for Historical Text**: By demonstrating the effectiveness of transformer-based embeddings on historical documents with OCR noise and linguistic variation, the study establishes best practices for applying modern NLP to historical corpora.

**Dynamic Topic Evolution**: The temporal analysis capability provides historians with unprecedented tools for tracking discourse evolution, moving beyond static snapshots to dynamic narratives of public opinion change.

**Embedding Quality vs. Model Size**: The finding that embedding quality matters more than model size provides practical guidance for researchers working with computational constraints.

## Limitations and Future Directions

The authors acknowledge several limitations that point toward future research directions:

**Topic Granularity**: BERTopic sometimes produces overly specific topics that could benefit from merging. Future work could incorporate soft clustering approaches or semi-automated topic consolidation.

**Visualization Enhancement**: While the temporal plots effectively show topic evolution, more sophisticated visualization techniques could improve interpretability for domain experts.

**Cross-linguistic Analysis**: The current approach relies on translation to English, potentially losing linguistic nuances. Future research could explore multilingual embedding models that preserve original language characteristics.

**Evaluation Metrics**: The study relies primarily on coherence and diversity metrics. Developing evaluation frameworks that better capture historical relevance and interpretability could strengthen the methodology.

## Significance and Impact

This research establishes a new standard for automated historical insight extraction, with implications extending across multiple disciplines. For Digital Humanities, it provides historians with scalable tools for analyzing vast textual archives while maintaining contextual depth. The demonstrated ability to track discourse evolution offers unprecedented opportunities for understanding how public opinion responds to major events and cultural shifts.

For computational linguistics, the study validates transformer-based approaches on challenging real-world historical data, providing evidence of their robustness to linguistic variation and OCR noise. The hyperparameter optimization findings offer practical guidance for implementing neural topic models efficiently.

The methodology's applicability extends beyond historical analysis to policy research, social science, and any domain requiring large-scale textual analysis with temporal components. The specific focus on nuclear discourse provides valuable insights for nuclear studies and policy analysis, demonstrating how public understanding of nuclear technology evolved across decades of technological development and major incidents.

By establishing BERTopic as an effective tool for historical text analysis and providing comprehensive evaluation frameworks, this research opens new avenues for computational approaches to understanding the past, promising to transform how historians and social scientists engage with textual archives in the digital age.

zh.title: 基于神经主题模型的大规模报纸档案历史洞察自动化提取
zh.abstract:
从大量非结构化历史报纸档案中提取连贯且易于理解的主题，由于主题演变、光学字符识别 (OCR) 噪声以及文本的海量性，面临着重大挑战。传统的LDA（隐含狄利克雷分布）等主题建模方法，在捕捉历史文本中话语的复杂性和动态性方面往往力有不逮。为解决这些局限性，我们采用了BERTopic。这种神经网络主题建模方法利用基于Transformer的嵌入来提取和分类主题，尽管其日益普及，但在历史研究中仍未得到充分利用。

我们的研究重点关注1955年至2018年间发表的文章，特别考察了有关核电和核安全的论述。我们分析了语料库中各种主题分布，并追溯它们的时间演变，以揭示公众话语中的长期趋势和转变。这使我们能够更准确地探索公众话语中的模式，包括核电与核武器相关主题的共现，以及它们随时间推移在主题重要性上的变化。

我们的研究展示了BERTopic作为传统方法的替代方案，在扩展性和语境敏感性方面的优势，为从报纸档案中提取的历史论述提供了更丰富的见解。这些发现为历史学、核研究和社会科学研究做出了贡献，同时反思了当前的局限性，并提出了未来工作的潜在方向。

summary.summary: 卢森堡大学的研究人员开发了一个名为BERTopic的神经网络主题建模框架，旨在从大型数字化报纸档案中自动提取和追踪连贯的历史主题。该方法在主题连贯性和多样性方面始终优于传统的经典主题模型，有效地阐明了围绕核事故等重大事件的公众舆论的时间演变。
originalProblem: 传统主题模型（如LDA、NMF）在捕捉历史文本中复杂、动态的论述和深层语义关系方面存在局限性，经常产生过于宽泛的主题。
对海量非结构化历史报纸档案进行人工分析，耗时费力，且在识别长期趋势时难以保证可扩展性和客观性。
现有计算方法通常对数字化历史文献中普遍存在的语言变异、固有偏见和OCR噪声敏感。
solution: 实施了BERTopic，一个利用基于Transformer的嵌入（GTE和Jina）和层次聚类（UMAP、HDBSCAN）实现上下文敏感文档表示的神经网络主题建模框架。
通过时间元数据扩展了BERTopic，以实现动态主题建模，从而追踪和可视化特定历史时期内的主题演变。
对包含超过14.8万篇历史报纸文章的大型语料库进行了全面的数据预处理，包括多语言翻译成英语、语言清理和优化。
keyInsights: 神经网络主题模型，特别是带有Transformer嵌入的BERTopic，在历史文本分析方面比经典模型更有效，因为它们能捕获更丰富的语义上下文并生成更连贯的主题。
嵌入模型的质量和上下文能力对于稳健的主题连贯性和多样性至关重要，其影响力往往超过模型本身的规模。
利用BERTopic进行的动态主题建模有效地揭示了公众舆论随时间推移的变化，从而能够识别与重大历史事件相对应的讨论高峰。
results: BERTopic在各项定量指标上始终优于经典的LDA和NMF模型，表现出卓越的主题连贯性和多样性，同时提高了计算效率。
动态主题分析成功识别并可视化了与哈里斯堡事故（1979年）、切尔诺贝利灾难（1986年）和福岛危机（2011年）等历史事件相关的公众舆论的明显激增。
该框架处理了1955年至2018年间发布的超过14.8万篇文章的大型语料库，展现了对复杂历史数据集的强大可扩展性和鲁棒性。

zh.overview:
## 概述

本研究提出了一项综合性研究，应用神经网络主题模型自动从大规模数字化报纸档案中提取历史见解。这项工作解决了传统文本分析方法在处理大量历史文献时所面临的基本局限性，展示了现代神经网络方法如何为公共话语演变提供更细致、更具时间意识的分析。

![方法论概述](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2512.11635v1/img-0.jpeg)
*图1：完整的方法论工作流程，展示了从数据收集到静态和动态主题建模的各个阶段，包括预处理、嵌入生成和评估阶段。*

## 问题与动机

历史文本分析传统上依赖于人工方法，尽管这些方法能提供深入的语境理解，但在面对“大数据”集合时，其规模和效率受到固有限制。经典的计算方法，如潜在狄利克雷分配（LDA）和非负矩阵分解（NMF），提供了一定的自动化，但存在显著缺点：它们需要预定义主题数量，难以处理语境细微差别，对数字化历史文档中常见的OCR噪声敏感，并依赖于词袋表示，无法捕获语义关系。

本研究的动机在于利用神经网络主题模型，特别是BERTopic，来克服这些局限性。神经网络方法利用基于Transformer的嵌入生成语境化表示，根据语境而非简单的词语共现来捕获语义。这种语境敏感性对于理解细致的历史话语以及追踪语言和主题如何随时间演变至关重要。

## 数据集和方法论

本研究使用了来自“impresso: Media Monitoring of the Past”项目的精选数据集，包含1955年至2018年间发表的超过148,000篇数字化报纸文章和广告。语料库特别关注核电和核安全话语，为分析围绕这些关键主题的公众舆论演变提供了丰富的材料。

该方法论涉及几个关键阶段：

**数据准备**：文档按时间段划分为四个时期（1955-1970年，1971-1986年，1987-2002年，2003-2018年）。原始的法语、德语和卢森堡语文本使用Google翻译译为英语。全面的预处理包括去噪、使用spaCy进行语言处理（停用词移除、分词、词形还原），以及过滤掉少于20个词符的文档。

**神经嵌入**：该方法利用句子Transformer模型，特别是来自Hugging Face的“gte-base-en-v1.5”和“jina-embeddings-v2-base-en”，这些模型因其捕获语义关系的能力以及处理长序列（最多8,192个词符）的能力而被选中。

**BERTopic实现**：核心方法论采用BERTopic，它将基于Transformer的嵌入与层次聚类相结合。该过程包括：
- UMAP（均匀流形近似与投影）用于在保留局部结构的同时进行降维
- HDBSCAN（分层密度聚类）用于对相似文档进行聚类，无需预定义聚类数量
- C-TF-IDF（基于类别的词频-逆文档频率）通过为每个聚类提供代表性词语进行主题表示

同时实施了静态主题建模（用于整体主题分析）和动态主题建模（结合时间元数据来追踪演变）。

## 主要发现

研究表明，在多个评估维度上，神经网络方法明显优于传统方法：

**定量性能**：BERTopic 在主题连贯性、主题多样性和计算效率方面始终优于经典方法（LDA、NMF 及其 TF-IDF/NER 变体）。GTE 嵌入模型表现尤为出色，而 Jina 嵌入虽然更紧凑，但提供了可媲美的结果。

**超参数优化**：有趣的是，使用 Parzen 树估计器（TPE）进行超参数优化仅提供了适度的改进，却需要大量的计算资源（在 GPU 上超过 24 小时）。这一发现表明 BERTopic 的默认配置是稳健且通常足够的，尤其是在资源受限的情况下。

**嵌入模型差异**：定性分析显示，不同的嵌入模型强调不同的主题方面。GTE 嵌入更侧重于技术、法律和政治维度，而 Jina 嵌入则强调地缘政治和环境问题。这表明嵌入选择可以根据特定的研究兴趣进行调整。

**时间分析能力**：动态建模组件被证明特别有价值，成功识别并可视化了重大历史事件周围的话语高峰。分析捕捉到了：

$$
\text{事件影响} = f(\text{主题频率}, \text{时间}, \text{历史背景})
$$

检测到的著名事件包括哈里斯堡事故（1979年）、切尔诺贝利灾难（1986年）、广岛50周年纪念（1995年）和福岛危机（2011年）。每个事件都显示出独特的时序模式，反映了公众反应的性质和规模。

## 技术创新

本研究对计算历史领域做出了几项技术贡献：

**历史文本的上下文嵌入**：通过证明基于 Transformer 的嵌入在带有 OCR 噪声和语言变异的历史文档上的有效性，本研究为将现代自然语言处理应用于历史语料库建立了最佳实践。

**动态主题演变**：时间分析能力为历史学家提供了前所未有的工具来跟踪话语演变，从静态快照转向公众舆论变化的动态叙事。

**嵌入质量与模型大小**：嵌入质量比模型大小更重要的发现为受计算限制的研究人员提供了实用指导。

## 局限性与未来方向

作者承认了一些局限性，这些局限性指出了未来的研究方向：

**主题粒度**：BERTopic 有时会产生过于具体的主题，这些主题可以受益于合并。未来的工作可以结合软聚类方法或半自动化主题整合。

**可视化增强**：虽然时间图有效地显示了主题演变，但更复杂的视觉化技术可以提高领域专家的可解释性。

**跨语言分析**：当前方法依赖于翻译成英语，可能会丢失语言细微差别。未来的研究可以探索多语言嵌入模型，以保留原始语言特征。

**评估指标**：本研究主要依赖于连贯性和多样性指标。开发更好地捕捉历史相关性和可解释性的评估框架可以加强方法论。

## 意义和影响

这项研究为自动化历史洞察提取树立了新标准，其影响范围延伸至多个学科。对于数字人文领域，它为历史学家提供了可扩展的工具，用于分析浩瀚的文本档案，同时保持上下文深度。所展示的追踪话语演变的能力为理解公众舆论如何响应重大事件和文化转变提供了前所未有的机会。

对于计算语言学而言，本研究验证了基于Transformer的方法在具有挑战性的真实历史数据上的表现，提供了它们对语言变异和OCR噪声鲁棒性的证据。超参数优化的发现为高效实现神经主题模型提供了实用指导。

该方法的适用性超越了历史分析，延伸到政策研究、社会科学以及任何需要大规模文本分析和时间成分的领域。对核话语的特别关注为核研究和政策分析提供了宝贵见解，展示了公众对核技术的理解如何经历了数十年的技术发展和重大事件而演变。

通过将BERTopic确立为历史文本分析的有效工具并提供全面的评估框架，本研究为理解过去的计算方法开辟了新途径，有望改变历史学家和社会科学家在数字时代处理文本档案的方式。

abstract: Extracting coherent and human-understandable themes from large collections of unstructured historical newspaper archives presents significant challenges due to topic evolution, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) noise, and the sheer volume of text. Traditional topic-modeling methods, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), often fall short in capturing the complexity and dynamic nature of discourse in historical texts. To address these limitations, we employ BERTopic. This neural topic-modeling approach leverages transformerbased embeddings to extract and classify topics, which, despite its growing popularity, still remains underused in historical research. Our study focuses on articles published between 1955 and 2018, specifically examining discourse on nuclear power and nuclear safety. We analyze various topic distributions across the corpus and trace their temporal evolution to uncover long-term trends and shifts in public discourse. This enables us to more accurately explore patterns in public discourse, including the co-occurrence of themes related to nuclear power and nuclear weapons and their shifts in topic importance over time. Our study demonstrates the scalability and contextual sensitivity of BERTopic as an alternative to traditional approaches, offering richer insights into historical discourses extracted from newspaper archives. These findings contribute to historical, nuclear, and social-science research while reflecting on current limitations and proposing potential directions for future work.

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models rely on retrieved evidence to guide large language model (LLM) generators, yet current systems treat retrieval as a weak heuristic rather than verifiable evidence. As a result, LLMs answer without support, hallucinate under incomplete or misleading context, and rely on spurious evidence. We introduce a training framework that treats the entire RAG pipeline -- both the retriever and the generator -- as an interactive proof system via an adaptation of the Merlin-Arthur (M/A) protocol. Arthur (the generator LLM) trains on questions of unkown provenance: Merlin provides helpful evidence, while Morgana injects adversarial, misleading context. Both use a linear-time XAI method to identify and modify the evidence most influential to Arthur. Consequently, Arthur learns to (i) answer when the context support the answer, (ii) reject when evidence is insufficient, and (iii) rely on the specific context spans that truly ground the answer. We further introduce a rigorous evaluation framework to disentangle explanation fidelity from baseline predictive errors. This allows us to introduce and measure the Explained Information Fraction (EIF), which normalizes M/A certified mutual-information guarantees relative to model capacity and imperfect benchmarks. Across three RAG datasets and two model families of varying sizes, M/A-trained LLMs show improved groundedness, completeness, soundness, and reject behavior, as well as reduced hallucinations -- without needing manually annotated unanswerable questions. The retriever likewise improves recall and MRR through automatically generated M/A hard positives and negatives. Our results demonstrate that autonomous interactive-proof-style supervision provides a principled and practical path toward reliable RAG systems that treat retrieved documents not as suggestions, but as verifiable evidence.
